shortLead: I build software with AI agents. The harness is everything around them: how I split work into sessions, the checks that decide whether work is right, and the memory that carries what we learn. I judge it by seven metrics: throughput, efficiency, token count, token cost, time taken, quality of output and hallucinations. This edition says what limits each one, what we have measured, and every idea we have against it, including the ones we only talked about.
ask: **What I need from you.** Read this page and Part 4, take a package (two people can share one) and write your name in its row. Parts 2 and 3 give the background for your package, and the reference edition holds every bottleneck and idea behind it.

p1.lead: FixFlow is the product. The harness is how we build it: everything we wrap around the AI models to build software with them. The word comes from software testing, where a test harness is the code that runs the tests; teams that build with AI agents now use it for the whole system around a model.
harness: **Sessions and agents.** A session is one conversation with Claude Code, Anthropic’s coding tool, which reads and edits code and runs commands on our PC. A session can start **subagents** (helpers that each begin with a fresh context) and **workflows** (scripts that run many subagents to a fixed plan).
**Checks and gates.** The test runs and reviews that decide whether a piece of work is good enough to merge into the main line of code.
**Memory.** Whatever carries what we learned from one session to the next: notes, the library we have designed, the knowledge store.

**The token budget.** A **token** is the unit a model reads and writes in, a short piece of text. The **context window** is everything the model holds in mind for one call, and it re-reads the whole window on every call. Our Claude plan allows a limited amount of use in each five-hour window, so tokens are the resource every part of the harness shares.
**The machine.** The one PC everything runs on: its power, memory, disk and Docker (the tool that runs our databases and Linux test runs in containers).
**How results reach me.** Reports, visual pages and decision forms.
p1.sources: Two of our own projects feed this record. **FixFlow** is the workshop management system we are building for a home-appliance repair shop in Karachi: a web app for the manager, an Android app for technicians and a backend in FastAPI (a Python web framework). Its build is laid out in the **ship plan**, the document that orders FixFlow’s work into phases (P0a, P0b and on). **The clinic testbed** is an earlier large build on this same PC that we used to push the harness hard: 432 commits and 65 merges in eight working days [M]. Most of our measured bottlenecks come from its record. Two outside sources were studied card by card: talks and writing by **Dex Horthy** of HumanLayer, and **BAML**, BoundaryML’s language for typed model calls. This edition also draws on what I typed in 59 [M] saved sessions since 6 October, because some ideas were only ever said in chat.
p1.arch: On 11 November we put what we had learned into one design, **harness v2**. It treats the harness as one system with four scarce things: time on the check, review, the one-at-a-time merge, and tokens per five-hour window. Each scarce thing gets a part that controls it.
p1.loops: The loop labels come from **system dynamics**, the method Jay Forrester began at MIT in the 1950s for studying systems as stocks, flows and feedback. A reinforcing loop (R) feeds itself: more of it makes more of it. A balancing loop (B) pushes back toward a limit.
p1.loopsNote: The blue labels are the loops of harness v2: R marks one that feeds itself, B one that pushes back toward a limit. Part 2 gives each its numbers under the bottleneck it belongs to.

p2.lead: A bottleneck is whatever limits one of the seven metrics I judge this work by. Most of them limit any team that builds with AI agents; the troubles of our own PC come last. This part gives where we stand on each metric, then each bottleneck with what we measured and the ideas we have against it, including the ideas that until now lived only in our chats.
p2.metricsLead: One row per metric: what it means, our best numbers today, the bottleneck I judge limits it most (numbered as in the blocks below) and what we cannot yet measure. Quality and hallucinations have catches but no rate yet.
p2.matrixLead: Agents sorted every bottleneck in the register and every idea by the metric it moves and by its cause. The causes group into the eleven bottlenecks below.
p2.matrixCap: Sorted by eight classifier agents on 14 November [E]. A blind second reading of 101 records agreed on the main metric for 80 and on the cause for 86 [M]. A bottleneck counts once for each metric it limits, and seven register rows have two causes, so they sit in two rows. A cell counts records, not how large each one is.
p2.blocksLead: Each block names the metrics the bottleneck limits (the two it limits most are filled in), says what happens, what we measured and what we have not, then lists ideas against it with how far each has got. Blocks 1 to 10 hold for any team building with AI agents; block 11 is our own PC and plan.
p2.leversShows: Every lever is a change to how we run sessions, not a new tool. A bare cap on the window is not enough for me: it saves tokens now and costs more later, as mistakes and summary problems surface. A 300–400k [T] window must carry an 800k [T] history (TOK-16). My proposal is to reach lever 1 by splitting sessions at a line (PAR-22). WP12’s replay puts 36.8 to 65.1 % [M] of what our sessions re-read past lines of 500k to 300k; the split is not yet tested live, and I said yes to one trial wave at 300k.
p2.splitCap: My proposal of 14 November (PAR-22). Rule, replay, their check and the trial’s set-up: `docs/program/SPLIT-RULE-2026-11.md`. Left panel: register rows B04 and PR-SUMMARY. Tree fills are illustrative [I]; the 40 % line is an outside rule of thumb [S], unmeasured (TK-FILL).
p2.splitShows: **The rule is written (WP12).** A session past the line hands its work to two fresh sessions (one, if it cannot be cut), each started from a one-page brief that points at the repository: finished material never enters it (TOK-44), and compaction is only a backstop. An inner session’s window still grows, so it too is replaced at the line, from its key table, and I open each new root.
p2.gridShows: Every one of the 21 has a home in the first four phases, a first step and a test that will show whether it is solved.
p2.matrixShows: Quality is limited from every direction: all eleven rows touch it. Hallucinations come mostly from one, claims accepted without a check (14 [E]). Token count sits mostly in three rows (context growth, the fixed start, finding and re-reading), and throughput and time mostly in three others (one orchestrator, the check, our own PC). 94 [E] of the 130 [M] bottlenecks and 381 [E] of the 484 [M] ideas would hold for any team building with AI agents.

p4.lead: Sixteen packages between them carry every bottleneck in the register and every idea in Part 3. Six can start today, one has begun (WP12), six start the day I give my word, and three follow another package. Read the box under the map before you take one.
p4.packages: One row per package. Each size carries its tag: [E] where a design estimated it, [G] where it is my guess until the first step reports; a package not yet sized says so. “Moves” names the two metrics most of the package’s ideas aim at. Write your name in the owner column when you take one. Two people can share a package; one person should not hold two packages from the same start column (today, on my word, after another package). The reference edition has a full card for each package, with the bottlenecks and ideas it carries and the kind of person it suits.
p4.decisions: Every open decision the package rows name, in one place; go-aheads and permission yeses without an id are in each package’s “Waits on me”. The reference edition gives the options for each and the one the source design recommends. I answered D01 to D06 on 11 November and merged PR #185 on 13 November; only D05’s power-cut notes are still to come.
p4.mapShows: The left column needs no decision from me, no agents and no Docker gate for its first deliverable, though any later step that launches agents waits on D07; the middle column waits on my word and the right one on another package.

howMade: The reference edition came first, following our orchestration design: Sonnet agents extracted every idea, bottleneck and term from the sources with a citation each, fresh-context Opus agents checked the records and every number, and nine fresh readers read the draft. On 14 November I changed the lens to the seven metrics and asked for the ideas that lived only in chat. Agents then read all 376 [M] messages I typed in 59 [M] saved sessions and matched 113 [M] ideas, observations and requests against the records: 5 [M] were in no record, and the earlier short edition had cut 31 [M] more. Eight classifier agents sorted all 606 [M] earlier records by metric, and a blind second reading agreed on the main metric for 80 of 101 [M]. Each block of Part 2 was written from its records and checked number by number by a second agent. Four fresh readers then read this edition, one of them against my own message line by line, and skeptics kept 49 [M] of their 73 [M] findings. A final check, against my message and against the records, kept 6 [M] of its 10 [M] findings, four [M] separate errors, all corrected here. The same day WP12 wrote the split rule and replayed it over our record, with two rounds of independent checking, and this edition carries the result.

themes.summary: Everything we build runs on one PC that powers off unexpectedly, and the clinic testbed still lives only there. Separate worktrees already pay: when the power went on 13 November, all eight [M] FixFlow lanes resumed from their own copies. Next, WP1 copies the work off the PC nightly, adds a resume list and an always-on sensor logger to find the cause.

key.name: Commit and push at every green checkpoint
key.line: Lanes commit and push at every checkpoint where checks pass, and the gate scripts treat locks older than the last boot as dead. In use since the 28-minute [M] outage.

key.name: Shutdown diagnosis and always-on sensor logger
key.line: Our logs showed 15 of 25 [M] shutdowns since 1 October with no Claude call shortly before, so our load alone does not explain them. The logger is allowed, not yet installed.

key.name: Off-machine copy of the work
key.line: A verified git bundle of every branch plus uncommitted work and transcripts, copied off the PC nightly. Designed; the first copy comes after I plug in the encrypted drive (D02).

themes.line: Everything we build runs on one PC that powers off unexpectedly, and the clinic testbed still lives only there.

themes.summary: The check decides whether work can merge, so it must be fast, fair and never pass when it tested nothing. Running tests in parallel took the clinic check from 855.2 s [M] to 283.8 s [M]; FixFlow’s gate harness uses several of these ideas daily. Next, WP2a runs the container and Windows checks side by side, measuring the peak memory that sizes the check slots.

key.name: Parallel check with one database per worker
key.line: Tests run in parallel workers, each with its own PostgreSQL test database, plus a serial pass for race tests. In use in the testbed: the full check averages 283.8 s [M].

key.name: Skip-aware integration gate
key.line: Integration tests run against the real database; a script fails the gate if any was skipped, so a missing database setting cannot go unnoticed. In use in every FixFlow backend gate run.

key.name: Linux container check, proposed as the gate
key.line: A Linux container runs the check, faster than on Windows, and it found 2 failures [M] Windows missed. Built in the testbed; I decide in D09 whether it becomes the gate.

themes.line: The check decides whether work can merge, so it must be fast, fair and never pass when it tested nothing.

themes.summary: In the clinic testbed a slice took 2.8 [M] review rounds on average, and in most high-risk merges nobody read the final commit. Opus review already works: it found a serious defect in 9 of 14 [M] Opus-built clinic slices. Next, WP3 moves the mechanical part of review into scripts that spend no tokens, starting with the replay seal and transcript audit.

key.name: Two-level merge gates with refute-reviewers
key.line: The root runs the full check and read-only Opus reviewers try to refute claims. In use for every testbed slice: it caught 19 [M] high-severity (P1) findings in round one.

key.name: Close findings only on tests with positive controls
key.line: A finding closes only on a test the harness runs, and every “nothing found” check needs a case it must find. In use in the testbed; a FixFlow trial is proposed.

key.name: Transcript audit at each merge
key.line: A read-only script over our session transcripts shows whether a reviewer read the final head. Built; its testbed run used 0 [M] model calls. WP3 builds the merge-time version first.

key.name: Fix-round contract: two rounds, revert, test per finding
key.line: Each finding needs a fail-before, pass-after test, and a failed fix is reverted, not patched over. Designed, not yet run; it starts with a replay on recorded fix chains.

themes.line: In the clinic testbed a slice took 2.8 [M] review rounds on average, and in most high-risk merges nobody read the final commit.

themes.summary: More lanes help only up to the knee; past it they add queues, tokens and collisions. Since 13 November FixFlow runs a coordinator session with one lane session per phase, and all eight [M] lanes resumed after a power loss. Next, WP4 replays the plan check on FixFlow’s first lane wave: where lanes would collide and the lane count it would have chosen.

key.name: Lane sessions: one phase, own worktree, run together
key.line: Each lane is an Opus-led session in its own worktree, taking a single phase to a draft PR. In use in FixFlow; RAM, not CPU, sets the lane ceiling [M].

key.name: Per-checkout isolation of worktree, port and database
key.line: Each checkout gets its own worktree, branch, port and database, and a second, simultaneous check of it is refused. In use in the testbed, where it supported 65 merges [M].

key.name: Plan check with footprints and collision graphs
key.line: Each slice declares its footprint, the files it will write; the plan check maps collisions and refuses overlapping writes. Designed in harness v2, not yet run on a real plan.

themes.line: More lanes help only up to the knee; past it they add queues, tokens and collisions.

themes.summary: Almost all our context tokens are re-reads of a window the model already read, so what we manage is calls times window size. Today each phase starts in a fresh session and Opus sessions compact earlier: 84 of the 117 [M] compactions in session windows are Opus, 81 [M] of them at 366–385k tokens. Next, WP5 proposes the token budget per five-hour window (D07), then puts the four levers to work.

key.name: Earlier auto-compact window
key.line: Compacts sessions earlier so later calls carry a smaller window. In use for Opus; Sonnet sessions ran to 963k [M], and a Sonnet trial waits on my D22.

key.name: One token budget: two lanes at a time
key.line: Two lanes at a time, each step written to disk. In use in the testbed; one five-hour window took about 3.4M [M] subagent tokens, the starting point for my D07 budget figure.

key.name: Strip fixed prefix with a short tool list
key.line: A short tool list, with tool descriptions loaded only when needed, aims to shrink the fixed start every agent re-reads (about 70,000 tokens [M] in the testbed). Designed; D18 waits on a with-and-without test.

themes.line: Almost all our context tokens are re-reads of a window the model already read, so what we manage is calls times window size.

themes.summary: Every new session starts without what the last one learned. For state, the repository passed its first test: a fresh agent recovered the facts from it alone. For lessons, the library and the knowledge store are designed, not built; next come the library’s limitation list (WP6a) and the store’s recurrence audit, which counts repeated problems (WP6b).

key.name: Short disciplined notes file as context memory
key.line: A short notes file, kept current and read to resume. Tested in a small, interrupted clinic study: recall 15 of 15 [M], matching both other arms; new mechanisms must beat it.

key.name: Fresh-agent cold-resume trial
key.line: A fresh Sonnet agent must recover frozen facts from the repository alone. Tested once: it recovered 10 of 10 [M] and exposed plan defects to fix; next, re-run at later phases.

key.name: Real-case walkthroughs of the library design
key.line: Agents walked real cases through the library’s design steps. Tested on 59 [M] chosen cases: 69 limitations [M], showing where it breaks, not how often. Next, we agree the list.

key.name: Knowledge store of solved problems (PR #183)
key.line: Stores hard solved problems, traps and failed approaches; a cheap agent looks them up by symptom. Designed, not built; next, the recurrence audit counting repeats (KS-D1), then my build decision (KS-D1b).

themes.line: Every new session starts without what the last one learned.

themes.summary: Before an agent changes code, it must find what the change touches. In a test on held-out FixFlow commits, with no agent in the loop, the typed code store reached recall 0.700 [M], ahead of scripted search; the gain sits in the mobile app. Next comes the zero-token index replay (WP7), then a test with an agent, once I settle GT-1.

key.name: Typed symbol-level graph of the repo
key.line: A model-free script maps the repo’s symbols and typed links. Tested on held-out commits without an agent: recall 0.700 [M], ahead of scripted search; the gain sits in the mobile app.

key.name: Same-facts cross-check between engines
key.line: Engines given the same facts must agree; a mismatch is a bug. In use: ours agreed on 770 of 770 [M] tasks, so we can choose one on speed, size and effort.

key.name: Agent-in-the-loop pilot
key.line: A fixed agent replays fix commits with and without SQL, graph or BM25 tools, counting tokens and success. An idea, not yet run; it follows the index replay, once I settle GT-1.

themes.line: Before an agent changes code, it must find what the change touches.

themes.summary: Many agents work at once, so briefing, model choice and judging need one written method. Its core is in use: a main session plans and judges, cheaper models discover with citations and fresh-context reviewers try to refute; in one staged run, discovery covered 16/16 [M] areas. Next, WP10a starts with a save-as-run rule: every workflow saved as a script before it runs.

key.name: Staged workflows with judging gates
key.line: Cheap discovery, a judging gate, an Opus deep-dive, another gate, then the phase plan; the main session writes a record at each gate. In use; one deep-dive returned 139 [M] findings.

key.name: Model tiers by role, raise effort before tier
key.line: Haiku extracts, Sonnet maps and runs gates, Opus analyses and refutes, the main session judges. In use in FixFlow and the clinic testbed; cost per tier not yet measured.

key.name: Coordinator session that never implements
key.line: One session owns the plan, shared results and merge calls, dispatches reviews and never implements. In use; it lets 8 [M] lanes run at once; speed effect not yet measured.

key.name: Save-rule and run provenance
key.line: Each evidence folder keeps the workflow script as it ran and its arguments, so the run can be repeated and audited. Designed, not yet tested; WP10a writes the rule first.

themes.line: Many agents work at once, so briefing, model choice and judging need one written method.

themes.summary: A subagent inherits the session’s model and loads nothing unless told, so a simple lookup can run on our most expensive tier. Our skill packages and pinned FixFlow agents are merged (PR #185) but not yet run; in use today is local GPU transcription of talks, at 19–45× real time [M]. Next, WP10b adds a frontmatter CI check and tallies which skills fire.

key.name: Agent file: pinned model, tools, preloaded skill
key.line: Each agent file pins its model, tools and preloaded skill; the agent works read-only unless told and cites everything. Built: 11 fixflow agent definitions [M], merged 13 November; not yet run.

key.name: [owner] stop markers in agent procedures
key.line: Steps only I may do, such as deploys or live restores, carry an [owner] marker; the agent stops and hands me the exact command. Built into all 13 skills [M], untested.

key.name: CI check for skill and agent frontmatter
key.line: A Node CI step fails bad skill and agent frontmatter, such as a name that differs from its folder. Designed, not built; WP10b first runs it record-only, flagging without blocking.

themes.line: A subagent inherits the session’s model and loads nothing unless told, so a simple lookup can run on our most expensive tier.

themes.summary: To choose fixes we need numbers we can trust and tests that are fair to the idea they test. Every number in our program documents carries a tag for how sure we are, and a transcript tally found that, by one count, slice sessions used 66.4 % [M] of November’s tokens. Next, WP8 builds a tagged rate sheet from the record.

key.name: Token tally from session transcripts
key.line: Read-only scripts parse every session transcript, count each call once, and total tokens and compactions per group. Measured for October and November; a re-measurement agreed within 0.3 % [M].

key.name: Pre-registered, sealed held-out test protocol
key.line: Freeze the test sets, metric and smallest worthwhile difference before any arm exists. In use on the graph test; every arm lost 0.05 to 0.17 [M] recall from tuning to held-out.

key.name: Measured-rates table feeding planner and governor
key.line: Measured rates, such as check time and rounds per slice, updated each wave for the planner and governor. Designed, not yet tested; WP8 starts it, writing unknowns as unknown.

themes.line: To choose fixes we need numbers we can trust and tests that are fair to the idea they test.

themes.summary: In the clinic testbed, first-use gaps hid behind test data until the last day; nothing ran on a real host. The testbed’s local staging rig already rehearses deploy and restore on synthetic data, with a fresh virtual machine serving in 109 s [M]; FixFlow’s lab emulator boots on this PC. Next, WP9 adds a zero-seed walk to every gate, then a real-host rehearsal.

key.name: Local staging VM rig with drills
key.line: A script-built Debian virtual machine with re-runnable drills: deploy, upgrade, backup and restore, load, security probe. In use in the testbed on synthetic data; next, a fresh-VM restore with me present.

key.name: Volume load and page-speed drill
key.line: Times pages on growing synthetic data and fingerprints each page to prove a speed-up changed no figures. Measured in the testbed: slow pages fell to 0.1–0.5 s [M]; next, a load rerun.

key.name: Zero-seed first-use walk in every gate
key.line: On an empty database, each gate walks install, first user, tills, a real-shaped import, a transaction and close of day. Designed, not built; would add 2 to 3 minutes [E] per gate.

themes.line: In the clinic testbed, first-use gaps hid behind test data until the last day; nothing ran on a real host.

themes.summary: Work waits on my decisions, and I decide quickly when I can see the choice on one page. In use today: W0-results.md, our single working board, which tracked 8 running lanes [M] on 13 November, and decision cards that mark the option the design recommends. Next, WP11 joins every open decision into one board beside the shared run queue.

key.name: W0-results.md as the single working board
key.line: One file holds my P0a steps, my decisions with defaults and the lane board; unknowns are written as unknown, with the reason. In use in FixFlow.

key.name: Decision cards D01 to D23
key.line: Each card shows the options, the one the design recommends, the bottlenecks touched and my answer. In use: D01 to D06 are answered; D07, the token budget, follows P0a.

key.name: Ship plan first; my yes for outside actions
key.line: FixFlow’s P0a goes first; no hooks, installs, scheduled tasks, permission changes or outbound data without my decision, and no harness agents during a FixFlow phase. Adopted as a standing rule.

themes.line: Work waits on my decisions, and I decide quickly when I can see the choice on one page.

picks.name: The PC powers off without warning
picks.big: 24 power-offs, 7 Oct–10 Nov, 23 without crash code [M]; on 13 Nov a 28-minute outage cut eight lanes [M].
picks.unlocks: Next power-off names its cause; zero sleep-related events in 14 days [T]; every stop is cheap to recover.

picks.name: Usage limits stop every lane at once
picks.big: 14 limit episodes, 6–20 Oct [M]; ten lanes were stopped by the limit within about 15 minutes [M].
picks.unlocks: A governor slows lanes so the usage window lasts; resumes never pay again for finished agents.

picks.name: Memory is short on this PC
picks.big: Memory, not CPU, caps check slots and lanes; on 13 Nov FixFlow had 5.5–7.7 of 31 GB free with eight lanes [M].
picks.unlocks: Slot and lane counts from a table of who holds memory when under 2 GB [T] is free.

picks.name: Checks queue behind each other
picks.big: 19 recorded waits: median 409 s, longest 2,030 s [M]; a second slot’s 8 GiB never free in about 980 samples [M].
picks.unlocks: Median wait under a minute [T] and up to 1.8–1.9× check throughput [M] with a second slot.

picks.name: Fix rounds that create new defects
picks.big: 64 % of reviews sent a slice back, 2.8 rounds per slice [M]; fixes made at least 5 more P1 defects [M].
picks.unlocks: Review rounds that converge under a stop rule, with fewer new defects per finding fixed.

picks.name: Agent reports overstate what was done
picks.big: 20-plus recorded overstatements of tests, evidence or runs [M]; model re-checks did not stop them.
picks.unlocks: Claims a script can recheck, with false flags under 10 % [T]; the orchestrator stops re-verifying by hand.

picks.name: Final commits not yet read by a person
picks.big: All review is a model reading a model’s code; 5 of 6 high-risk final commits went unread [M].
picks.unlocks: Unread high-risk merges cut from 5 of 6 [M] to zero [T].

picks.name: One orchestrator is the serial gate
picks.big: One root session reviews, merges and runs checks, capping how fast work leaves; it took 15.3 % of November tokens [M].
picks.unlocks: No compaction across a wave of five gates [T]; the token gain is bounded by that share.

picks.name: Code phases waited on my P0a
picks.big: 37 of 56 phases wait behind P0a [M]; on 13 Nov production still answered Railway’s edge 404 [M].
picks.unlocks: Finishing P0a unblocks all work that reaches a phone or host; lanes build ahead until then.

picks.name: Work waits for me when I am away
picks.big: Restarts wait for me: Docker and sessions stay down; about three days idle after the 6 Nov power-off [M].
picks.unlocks: Time from “could resume” to next commit falls from about three days [M] to under three hours [T].

picks.name: Gaps found only on the last day
picks.big: Every clinic slice was tested on synthetic data; two [M] first-use gaps surfaced only on the final day.

before.title: Two projects, one PC: the ship plan first
before.text: Work on a branch, never on main, and never delay or edit FixFlow’s next phase for harness work. Before using the Docker gate or an agent, read the lane board (`docs/program/W0-results.md`) on PR #182’s plan branch: FixFlow phases running or awaiting review go first, as they share this PC’s memory and our usage limit.

before.title: One budget for the whole team
before.text: Two lanes at a time (your own session counts), a written token budget before any launch (D07) and one agent-adding change per five-hour window, shared by everyone. Stop launching after the first empty result, a possible usage limit. Book agent runs in WP11’s shared queue; until it exists, wait for my yes.

before.title: One limit on heavy checks
before.text: A heavy check from either project takes a slot from `ff-slot.sh`, FixFlow’s machine-wide lock. Its pools and slot counts stay as they are; WP2b may propose only how waiters are ordered.

before.title: The coordinator writes FixFlow’s program files
before.text: Changes to the ship plan, lane board or FixFlow’s gate scripts go to the coordinator as proposals; the coordinator brings them to me and writes them once I say go.

before.title: Machine traps that already cost us time
before.text: Never prune Docker networks or restart Docker; new networks get explicit subnets inside 10.77.0.0/16. Under `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV`, write `C:/…` paths. Clone with `core.longpaths`. No `python` on PATH; use Node. Never touch the antivirus.

points.h: The window keeps growing, and that is the first bottleneck.
points.t: Every call re-reads the whole window, so each step costs more than the last, and the orchestrator’s window reached 574k to 974k tokens [M] before it compacted. Both summaries we checked were then wrong about the latest state [M]. My proposal is to run orchestration as a B+ tree spread over sessions, as in a distributed system: a session past about 40 % [S] of its window (set per model) splits, small ones merge, and we may never have to compact. WP12 wrote the rule and replayed it on our record: tokens are not settled against compacting earlier, and its first aim, fewer hallucinations, needs a live trial. I said yes to one trial wave at 300k, ahead of most of our compactions.

points.h: Hallucinations and quality have catches, not yet a rate.
points.t: We recorded 20-plus overstated reports, with no denominator [M], and those two wrong summaries [M]. 64 % [M] of reviews sent a slice back, and an Opus reviewer found a serious defect in 9 of 14 [M] Opus-built slices. Two things should bring the numbers down: claims that a script rechecks instead of a model, and windows that stay small (not yet measured). A script rechecked 1,265 [M] paths, commits and pull requests in FixFlow’s summaries: 16 [M] were not borne out, no more than in maintained documents; the latest state needs a reader. WP8 counts reports next.

points.h: One orchestrator and one usage limit cap throughput.
points.t: Review, merging and checks all pass through one session, and when the five-hour limit hits, every lane stops: ten were stopped within about 15 minutes [M]. The testbed had about three lanes worth running [M] but ran six to nine [M]. The planner, the merge queue and the governor are designed to answer this.

points.h: Every agent pays a fixed start, often on the most expensive model.
points.t: About 70k tokens [M] per clinic agent before any work, 27 % [E] of all our tokens. A short tool list should shrink it; model tiers by role are in use, and raising only the stuck problem to the top model is designed but not yet measured.

points.h: Most steps only find and re-read.
points.t: 64 % [M] of FixFlow’s calls and 52 % [M] of the clinic’s only read or searched, each one a full re-read. A typed code store found more of what a change touched than a scripted search did (+0.076 overall [M], the gain in the mobile app). The test with an agent in the loop is next.

points.h: What one session learns, the next does not have.
points.t: The library and the knowledge store are designed, not built. The ensemble of simulated runs I suggested on 12 November helped: it showed which unknowns matter most. The same model’s corner settings (MEM-15) show the library pays only when work comes back, reaches the cheap model and is right, all together. Neither can pick a path, because the inputs are still guesses [G].

points.h: A lot already works, and the work splits cleanly.
points.t: The clinic’s full check is 3.0× faster in parallel [M] and 1.6× faster in a Linux container [M]. Sixteen packages each have a goal, a first deliverable and a “done when”: one has begun, six can start today, six start on my word and three follow another package.

blocks.title: The window keeps growing until it must compact or clear

hits.how: Every call re-reads the whole window, so long sessions multiply tokens
Compaction summaries got the latest state wrong
Re-read context is billed again on every call
A compaction dropped an open loop of unfinished work

blocks.what: Every call re-reads the whole window and adds to it, so our orchestrator and long-lived sessions accumulate tokens until they must compact or clear. The summary that then replaces the history can misstate the latest state.
blocks.measured: Cache reads are 96.8 % [M] of 7.35 B [M] context tokens, output 0.75 % [M]. The root compacted at 574k, 974k, 967k and 970k tokens [M], though a second count of the same transcripts finds three compactions [M]. 2 of 2 summaries were wrong on the latest state [M]; the verbatim tail corrected both. Vendor figures, not reproduced here, put native compaction at 48.7 against 69.3 for the full history [S] (TOK-41). Our snapshot-and-restore trial matched native compaction on recall and task success but used 17.0 % more tokens [M] (TOK-12).
blocks.unmeasured: At what window fill a session’s judgement starts to fall, for any model, and whether a brief written at a split is right more often than a compaction summary.

ideas.name: Orchestration as a distributed B+ tree: split and merge
ideas.result: Designed: my idea of 14 November, aimed first at hallucinations. Rule written and replayed on our record (below), not tested live. I said yes to a 300k trial; old summaries are read first.

ideas.name: Take finished material out of a live window
ideas.result: Designed: asked for on 26 October, now settled inside the split rule. A new session starts from a brief that points at the repository, so finished material never enters it. Untested.

ideas.name: Compaction snapshot, restore and recall hooks
ideas.result: Built: in the clinic testbed, not yet run live. 85 offline tests [M], 53 defects fixed [M]. Restore quality not yet measured.

ideas.name: Earlier auto-compact window of 400,000 tokens
ideas.result: In use for Opus: 84 of the 117 [M] compactions in session windows are Opus, 81 [M] of them at 366–385k. Sonnet ran to 963k [M] and is not set yet.

blocks.title: Agent reports claim more than was actually done

hits.how: Reports cite tests, evidence or runs that do not exist
Green checks and unread final commits let defects through
I re-verify claims by hand instead of trusting them
Opus skeptics are spent re-checking what a script could

blocks.what: Agents report tests, evidence or runs that did not happen or do not match, and a model re-reading its own claims does not catch it. A check can also go green while testing nothing.
blocks.measured: 20-plus recorded overstatements, with no denominator [M]. 5 of 6 high-risk final commits went unread [M]. A citation check re-located 109 [M] claims, none dead, and 575 of 579 [M] quotes matched exactly.
blocks.unmeasured: What share of claims are false: overstatements are counted without a denominator yet.

ideas.result: Designed: confirmed needs a traced path, refuted needs counter-evidence, otherwise unverifiable with what would settle it. Not yet tested.

ideas.name: Citation check over every claim
ideas.result: In use: 109 [M] claims re-located, none dead; 575 of 579 [M] quotes matched exactly. It checks existence only.

ideas.name: Test-id accounting and planted-fault demos
ideas.result: In use: in the testbed, six planted faults gave CHECK FAILED [M], and no test id ran twice. Not yet in FixFlow CI.

ideas.name: Claims file checked by a script each round
ideas.result: Designed: a script reruns each cited test at parent and head. Not yet run. Replay first, false flags under 10 % [T].

blocks.title: One orchestrator reviews and merges everything, and its window overflows

hits.how: Every review and merge passes through one session, one at a time
One usage limit stops every lane together, mid-run
Every agent’s full report lands in the root’s window
Lanes sit waiting on the one session

blocks.what: One root session reviews, merges, edits the board and reads every agent’s report, so work leaves only as fast as it does. Its window keeps growing until it must compact, and one usage limit stops every lane together.
blocks.measured: Root compacted at 574k, 974k, 967k and 970k tokens [M] (a second count of the same transcripts finds three compactions [M]), about 499k per call [M], 15.3 % of November tokens [M]. Subagents made 91 of 104 limit errors [M]. Ten lanes were stopped by the limit within about 15 minutes [M].
blocks.unmeasured: Whether a gate workflow stops root compaction, and how cache reads count against the limit.

ideas.name: Bounded session tree: depth three, fan-out three
ideas.result: In use: my proposal of 2 November; 12 slices and about 20 follow-up branches merged in 8 days [M]. The root still became a serial gate; PAR-22 is its next form.

ideas.name: Planner that sizes lanes just below the knee
ideas.result: Designed: plan accepted 11 Nov, nothing installed. The testbed had about three lanes worth running [M] but ran six to nine [M].

ideas.name: Lane sessions: one phase, own worktree, run together
ideas.result: In use: eight lane sessions started on 13 November [M] and PRs #187–#192 opened that day [M]. RAM, not CPU, sets the ceiling [M].

ideas.name: Review as a gate workflow with typed verdict
ideas.result: Designed: gain is bounded, the root is 15.3 % [M] of tokens. Target: no root compaction across five gates [T].

blocks.title: Each agent pays a fixed start and may inherit the top model

hits.how: About 70k [M] tokens load before work, re-read every call
An unpinned lookup agent runs on the session’s model
Tiny fan-outs pay the prefix many times for little work

blocks.what: Every agent window first loads system prompt, tool and connector schemas, skills, memory, CLAUDE.md and its brief, then re-reads it every call. Fan-out multiplies it, and an unpinned agent inherits the session’s model, even for a simple lookup.
blocks.measured: About 70k [M] tokens per clinic agent before any work (about 60k [E] per FixFlow agent): tools 34k, connectors 17k, skills 9k, system 8k, memory 2k [M]. That fixed start is 27 % [E] of all our tokens and 47 % [E] of FixFlow’s.
blocks.unmeasured: What tiering and a stripped prefix actually save: no per-tier spend is recorded yet.

ideas.name: Escalation ladder: raise only the stuck problem a tier
ideas.result: Designed: on guessed inputs, 25.7 [G] cheap-call equivalents, 21.2 % [G] wrong, versus 29.9 [G] and 11.2 % [G] strong model alone.

ideas.name: Fast mode for a fleet of subagents
ideas.result: Proposed: fast mode was on for a 132 [M] agent run on 3 November. Effect on time and tokens not measured yet.

ideas.name: Strip the fixed prefix with a short tool list
ideas.result: Designed: tool definitions are 34k [M] of the 70,000 [M] each agent pays. Pass bar: 20 runs [T], zero refused writes.

ideas.name: Model tiers by role, raise effort before tier
ideas.result: In use: 12 [M] agent definitions pin Haiku, Sonnet or Opus. Tiering has no cost measurement yet.

blocks.title: Agents spend most calls just finding and re-reading things

hits.how: every lookup call re-reads the whole window
fetched file content fills windows and is re-processed every call
each extra lookup adds a whole model step

blocks.what: Over half our calls only read or search, and each call re-reads the whole window. Fetched file content stays and is re-processed every later call, and a small set of files recurs across sessions.
blocks.measured: FixFlow: 64 % [M] of calls, 55 % [M] of tokens only read or search. Fetched content fills 26 % [E] of windows; 72 paths [M] hold half. One model step takes 6,600 ms [M], a 93 KB file read 0.5 ms [M].
blocks.unmeasured: Whether any graph, map or recall aid makes an agent finish faster: 0 [M] agent runs.

ideas.name: Time model steps against disk reads
ideas.result: Tested: a model step takes 6,600 ms [M]; a file read 0.5 ms (possibly a warm read), a 618-file search 124 ms [M]. Count steps saved.

ideas.name: Typed symbol-level graph of the repo
ideas.result: Tested: recall 0.700 [M] vs 0.625 [M] for scripted search; the gain is on mobile (+0.151 [M]). No agent run yet.

ideas.name: Typed-edge map of the planning documents
ideas.result: Built: clinic testbed prototype, 3,361 records for 167 KB [M]; extraction recall 0.52 [M]. No agent has used it yet.

ideas.name: Batch lookups into one command
ideas.result: Proposed: batching two lookups would remove about a third of all calls [E] and a third of their re-reads [E].

blocks.title: Each session starts without what earlier sessions learned

hits.how: the same errors are re-hit across sessions and projects
fresh sessions can start from stale or contradictory facts
recurring hard problems are solved again at the top tier
drifted docs and memory state things no longer true

blocks.what: A new session knows only what the repo and memory files carry. Past diagnoses sit in prose nobody can search by symptom, so a recurring defect is solved again at the top tier, and docs drift from code.
blocks.measured: One missing-tool error was re-hit in 54 of 78 [M] sessions across 9 [M] projects. 3 to 5 [M] same-cause repeats among 48 [M] fix commits. 517 of 1,268 backticked file names in docs do not resolve [M]. A cold-resume trial recovered 10 of 10 frozen facts [M].
blocks.unmeasured: How often similar problems recur in our work, which decides whether a library pays.

ideas.name: Ensemble of simulated runs over the pathway map
ideas.result: Built: my suggestion in the library-pathways chat of 12 November. 1000 [S] runs per setting; 51 [M] of 60 [M] unknowns are guesses. It helped by ranking what to measure first. On those guesses the library was cheaper and no more wrong than the escalation ladder in only 0.3 % [G] of runs, or 6.1 % [G] when its unknowns move together, and the model shows it pays only when much work comes back, reach is high and entries are good (cost 0.82 [G], wrong 0.67 [G]; MEM-15). It cannot pick a path on guessed inputs. A trained tree ensemble (MEM-68) is not started.

ideas.name: Merge partial solutions through a graph
ideas.result: Proposed: not yet tested. In real walks two checked answers did not make a checked merge (6 cases [M]); tests will decide.

ideas.name: Knowledge store of solved problems
ideas.result: Designed: nothing built. Same-cause repeats are 3 to 5 [M] among 48 [M] fix commits; the recurrence audit decides whether to build.

ideas.name: Memory file holds pointers, not restated state
ideas.result: In use: memory now points to where state lives; the rewrite found and corrected one [M] stale next step.

blocks.title: Fixes create new defects and gaps surface late

hits.how: fix-made defects and late gaps reach review or the end
extra review rounds stretch every slice
slices sent back are not yet accepted work
each extra round spends review tokens again

blocks.what: A fix can add new stored state whose endings no test covers, so each fix round makes fresh defects and the rounds do not converge; ours did. Work tested only on synthetic data lets first-use gaps surface on the last day.
blocks.measured: Round one found 19 high-severity (P1) defects [M], and the fixes made at least 5 more P1 and 10 P2 [M]. 64 % of reviews sent a slice back, 2.8 rounds per slice [M]. Two [M] first-use gaps surfaced on the final day.
blocks.unmeasured: How many fix-made defects a two-round fix contract would prevent; its replay has not run yet.

ideas.name: Two-level merge gates with refute-reviewers
ideas.result: In use: every testbed slice; 9 of 11 [M] gates took three rounds, and fixes created at least 5 [M] more P1.

ideas.name: Fresh critics check each plan revision’s changes
ideas.result: Tested: the v6-to-v8 delta check found 1 blocker, 20 major, 20 minor [M] before work started; findings folded into the next version.

ideas.name: Fix-round contract: two rounds, revert, test per finding
ideas.result: Designed: not yet run. A replay on recorded defect chains would show whether it beats 2.8 [M] review rounds per slice.

ideas.name: One drift audit after ten PRs
ideas.result: Proposed: per-PR review cannot see drift that builds across PRs as the repo grows; one fresh Opus audit after the 10th [T] merged code PR, pass bar at least 2 [T] findings I accept. Not yet run.

blocks.title: Lanes queue behind one slow check slot

hits.how: Lanes sit idle waiting for a free check slot
One open slot caps how many lanes finish at once
Windows-only checks miss failures the Linux run catches

blocks.what: Every lane must pass the full check before merging, and checks share limited machine capacity, so lanes wait in line. On our PC, Windows also adds a slow hop to the database.
blocks.measured: 19 recorded waits: median 409 s, longest 2,030 s [M]. Parallel workers cut a full run from 855.2 s [M] to a mean of 283.8 s [M], about 3.0×. Two slots gave 1.8–1.9× throughput [M]. Linux container check: 230.1 s [M] against 367.2 s [M] on Windows.
blocks.unmeasured: One check’s peak memory, so we cannot yet size slots safely.

ideas.name: Parallel check with one database per worker
ideas.result: In use: 855.2 s [M] became a mean of 283.8 s [M], about 3.0× faster. Eight workers gain only 3 % [M].

ideas.name: Linux container check, proposed as the gate
ideas.result: Built: mean 230.1 s [M] against 367.2 s [M] native, about 1.6× faster, and found 2 failures [M] Windows missed.

ideas.name: Two container checks at once
ideas.result: Tested: 266 s and 267 s [M] together against about 440 s [M] in a row, least free memory 5.3 GB [M].

blocks.title: False statements and gains go uncounted, so fixes stay unproven

hits.how: No context aid tested with an agent, so payoff unknown
Wrong output is found only when someone happens to catch it
No rate per session, model or window fill exists
Levers cannot be judged without before-and-after token tallies

blocks.what: We learn of a false statement only when a reviewer, a script or I catch it, and no context aid has run with an agent in the loop. So we cannot yet tell whether a change helps.
blocks.measured: 20-plus recorded overstatements, with no denominator [M]; 2 of 2 compaction summaries wrong on the latest state [M]. A script rechecked 1,265 [M] paths, commits and pull requests in FixFlow’s 61 [M] recorded summaries: 16 were not borne out, 1.3 % [M], no more than in two maintained documents. 0 [M] agent runs with a context aid. November token tally: 4,252.9M [M] cache-read tokens; re-measurement agreed within 0.3 % [M].
blocks.unmeasured: Whether a fuller orchestrator window degrades its judgements; keeping context under about 40 % [S] is an outside rule of thumb.

ideas.result: In use: agents sorted all 606 [M] earlier records; a blind second reading agreed on the main metric for 80 of 101 [M].

ideas.name: Token tally from session transcripts
ideas.result: Tested: November counted 4,252.9M [M] cache-read tokens over 184 files; re-measurement agreed within 0.3 % [M]. Per-slice figures next.

ideas.name: Log context use at each phase close
ideas.result: Proposed: a usage line (tokens, percent, compactions) on the first 4 [T] phase sessions, so the split line rests on our own data.

blocks.title: Agents start without settled facts, defined values or tested skills
blocks.short: How we brief and equip agents

hits.how: Undefined severity values let a first impression harden into priority
Assessors redo work that was already settled programme law
Without settled facts, analysts fall back on hypotheses
Agents re-derive project facts each run instead of reading them

blocks.what: Agents were briefed before settled facts existed, output schemas leave values like P0–P3 undefined, and the new skill packages have not run yet. Agents re-derive facts, and a cheap first impression can become a priority.
blocks.measured: 8 of 12 skeptic verdicts in G2 lowered a severity [M]. 8 of 24 assessment adopts were already programme law [M]. Staged workflows work: discovery covered 16/16 [M] areas in 14 min [M]; the deep-dive gave 139 [M] findings in 23 min [M].

ideas.result: Built: 52 [M] research agents checked 44 [M] course series; a lecture list maps each harness problem to its lectures.

ideas.result: Tested: our structure served the BAML case as well or better on all ten dimensions (judged); borrows 10 to 40 lines [E].

ideas.name: Staged workflows with judging gates between them
ideas.result: In use: discovery covered 16/16 [M] areas in 14 min [M]; the deep-dive gave 139 [M] findings in 23 min [M].

blocks.title: Work stops when this PC fails or I am away
blocks.short: This PC and waiting on me

hits.how: Power-offs and hand restarts leave lanes idle for days
An outage cuts every lane off mid-work
Short memory caps how many lanes and slots can run

blocks.what: Everything runs on one PC that powers off without warning and is short of memory. After a stop, Docker, databases and sessions wait for me to restart them, and merges and starts wait for my approval.
blocks.measured: About three days idle after the 6 Nov power-off [M]. 25 shutdowns since 1 October [M], 15 with no Claude call ten minutes before [M]. After a 28-minute [M] outage all eight [M] lanes resumed from their worktrees. Dropping Docker’s cache gave back 2.2 GB [M].
